title: Timeline and Sources of History — Chapter Summary
intro: History is the story of the past, but the past is enormous. To make sense of it, historians do two things: they place events on a TIMELINE so they can see what came before and what came after, and they read SOURCES — old objects, writings and stories that survived from earlier times. This chapter teaches both ideas. You will learn how time is counted (BCE and CE), how Indian history is divided into broad periods, and how archaeologists, texts and oral traditions together let us know the past.

sections.heading: What a Timeline Shows
bullets: A timeline places events in the order they happened — earlier on the left, later on the right.
Spacing between events shows how far apart they were in time.
It shows ORDER (which came first).
It shows DURATION (how long an event or reign lasted).
It shows SIMULTANEITY (what was happening at the same time elsewhere).

sections.heading: Counting Years — BCE and CE
bullets: Year 1 CE is the reference point of the modern calendar.
Years before it are BCE; years after are CE.
Bigger BCE number = earlier (3000 BCE is older than 2000 BCE).
Bigger CE number = more recent (2000 CE is later than 1000 CE).
There is NO year zero — 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE.
Indian eras: Vikram Samvat began 57 BCE; Shaka Samvat began 78 CE.

sections.heading: Big Blocks of Time
bullets: Decade = 10 years.
Century = 100 years (the 21st century CE = 2001–2100).
Millennium = 1000 years.
Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age are named after the main material used for tools.
Indian history is broadly grouped into Ancient (up to ~700 CE), Medieval (~700–1700 CE) and Modern (~1700 CE onwards) — convenient labels, not sharp walls.

sections.heading: Three Families of Sources
bullets: Archaeological sources — physical objects that survived: pottery, tools, coins, beads, ruins, seeds, bones.
Literary sources — written texts: the Vedas, Mahābhārata, Rāmāyaṇa, Buddhist Tripiṭakas, Jaina Āgamas, Sangam poetry, inscriptions.
Oral sources — songs, stories, genealogies, proverbs passed by word of mouth across generations.
Each kind is partial — historians use MANY sources together and cross-check them.

sections.heading: Archaeology and Dating
bullets: Archaeologists excavate sites and study LAYERS of soil — older lies deeper (stratigraphy).
Radiocarbon (C-14) dating measures C-14 in once-living material (wood, charcoal, bone, seeds) to give an age.
Famous Indian sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal (Harappan); Pātaliputra (Mauryan); Sānchī (Buddhist); Hampi (Vijayanagara); Ajanta and Ellora caves.

sections.heading: Texts, Inscriptions and Coins
bullets: The four Vedas — Ṛig, Sāma, Yajur, Atharva — are the earliest Indian texts.
The two great epics are the Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa.
Buddhist Tripiṭakas (Pāli) and Jaina Āgamas (Prakrit) preserve their traditions.
Sangam literature (Tamil) gives a vivid picture of early South India.
Inscriptions are texts carved on stone, copper or pillars — Ashoka's edicts (3rd c. BCE) are the most famous.
Coins show kings' names, languages and symbols — and tell us about trade when found far from where they were minted.

sections.heading: Asking Questions of a Source
bullets: WHO made this source — a king, priest, traveller, craftsperson?
WHEN was it made — can we date it directly?
WHY was it made — to celebrate a king, to teach, to trade?
WHAT does it leave out — defeats, ordinary people, women?
Does ANOTHER source agree? Independent agreement is strong evidence.

key_takeaways: A timeline orders events and shows duration and simultaneity.
BCE/CE: bigger BCE = earlier; bigger CE = later; NO year zero.
Indian history: Ancient → Medieval → Modern, around 700 CE and 1700 CE as rough boundaries.
Three source families: archaeological (objects), literary (texts), oral (stories and songs).
Stratigraphy gives RELATIVE dates; radiocarbon dating gives ABSOLUTE dates for organic samples.
Famous sources include the Vedas, the epics, Tripiṭakas, Sangam poetry, Ashoka's edicts and ancient coins.
Good history uses many sources together and asks careful questions of each.

glossary.definition: A line on which events are placed in the order they happened, with spacing showing elapsed time.
Before Common Era — years before the reference year 1 CE; bigger BCE = older.
Common Era — years after the reference year 1 CE; bigger CE = more recent.
A period of one hundred years.
A period of one thousand years.
Any surviving evidence (object, text or story) used by historians to study the past.
The study of the past through material remains, especially through excavation of sites.
The study of layers (strata) at a site; deeper layers are older than the layers above them.
A scientific test that measures C-14 in once-living material to estimate its age in years.
A short text carved on stone, copper or a pillar, often at the time of the event.
The four earliest Indian sacred texts in Sanskrit — Ṛig, Sāma, Yajur and Atharva.
The three 'baskets' of Buddhist sacred texts, preserved in Pāli.
Early Tamil poetry from the early centuries CE, a major source for South Indian history.
Royal proclamations carved on rocks and pillars by Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.
